in_text_mentions: In 2011, a 52-year-old female presented with worsening of her longstanding severe bilateral foot pain. Initial radiographs are presented in Figures 1, 2 as anteroposterior and lateral views of the right ankle which demonstrate collapse of the navicular and secondary osteoarthritic changes. She was fitted with an orthosis; however, the disease process progressed. In 2014 the patient underwent an unsuccessful left talonavicular fusion with an iliac bone graft which was repeated in 2015 with a successful outcome.

in_text_mentions: Left foot weight-bearing radiographs (Figure 2) at presentation demonstrate many of the classic features of MWD. The posterior-anterior (PA) projection reveals a comma-shaped navicular, with relative collapse of the lateral half. The lateral radiograph suggests dorsal navicular fragmentation, with mild dorsal displacement of the dorsal fragment. It also confirms pes planus, with a Meary-Tomeno angle that is convex inferiorly. His lateral calcaneal column is relatively short compared with his talus. Using the radiographic staging system devised by Maciera et al, this is stage 4 disease (stage 5

MRI (Figure 2) at presentation showed bone marrow edema in the dorsal navicular fragment but, importantly, no significant reduction in T1 signal intensity to suggest osteonecrosis. It also confirmed the absence of perinavicular degenerative changes, with preserved talonavicular and naviculocuneiform joint cartilage. Adjacent soft tissues were evaluated, confirming normal appearances to the tibialis posterior tendon and the spring ligament.

Figures 1, 2 illustrate the weight-bearing AP, and the lateral views of the foot are shown. The intersection angle between the calcaneus and tibia was measured preoperatively and postoperatively in the calcaneus axis radiography; we named the novel angle the “calcaneus varus angle” (CVA) (varus = positive value, valgus = negative value) (Figure 3). The fusion was considered successful when the bon

nd effusion in adjacent joints (7, 8). We believed that there was a higher incidence for adjacent joint arthritis in the Stage IV MWD than in the earlier stages because pes planus foot happened in stage IV. CT and MRI can identify adjacent joint arthritis in the stage such as calcaneal cuboid bone arthritis (Figures 1, 2). As a result, three patients in our report were revealed with calcaneal cuboid joint arthritis by CT and MRI and underwent TN plus CC fusion, and had good clinical outcomes. Otherwise, the pathological changes in the calcaneal-cuboid joint could be neglected in the treatment.

The accompanying text explicitly notes the demonstration of navicular fragmentation, matching the finding key kohler_disease_fragmented_navicular. B: Panel B is a lateral radiograph of the patient's grandfather with MWD. The text notes appearances consistent with mechanical compression on the lateral navicular, classified as navicular collapse.

in_text_mentions: Interestingly, the patient's maternal grandfather also had MWD, which was severe and disabling for much of his life. He developed midfoot pain at age 10 years and had a pes planus deformity. He had radiographs in adulthood (Figure 4) which demonstrated fragmentation of the navicular and advanced perinavicular degenerative changes. Importantly, he had similar tarsal alignment to his grandson with a relatively short calcaneous and appearances in keeping with mechanical compression on the lateral navicular.
